# Baselines, datasets and the fair-comparison protocol {#sec-baselines}

**ISLA is measured against the two public slice-attention transformers
with the strongest record on industrial aerodynamics, GeoTransolver and
Transolver, on seven datasets, under one protocol that fixes everything
except the architecture.** The baselines are strong, not straw.
Each architecture runs at one reference configuration, the most accurate
of its architecture under one memory budget, and GeoTransolver receives raw
coordinates that ISLA never sees. Both baselines run at their own best
learning rate, and neither is ever modified. This chapter says what each baseline computes
and sees. It states one rule about how a problem's global conditions enter
any model, lists the protocol as twelve rules, and holds what is common to
every dataset: the roster, the file conventions and the split rule (each
dataset's own problem, conversion and standing are in its chapter of Part
III). It closes with the protocol table under which every
cross-architecture number in the book is produced.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"
meta = {p.stem: json.load(open(p)) for p in sorted(PF.glob("*.json"))}  # the problem-figure metadata of @tbl-data-samples
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's routing mechanism and differ in
what they are allowed to see: raw coordinates in a frame, and the problem's
global vector as a raw feature.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*. It pools point features into one
token per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the
result back through the same mixture. That is *physics attention*.
GeoTransolver adds a geometry encoder and a global-context projector.
@fig-family-diagram places ISLA beside them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-family-diagram
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   What each architecture is handed, and where they differ. Gray boxes
%%|   are data; the routing mechanism (solid blue) is shared by the whole
%%|   family. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive coordinates in the
%%|   dataset's frame and the global vector as a vector; ISLA receives only
%%|   invariants of the same inputs and its slices carry the surface measure
%%|   (dashed blue: fixed maps with no parameters). How to read this: the
%%|   diagram shows inputs and structure, not accuracy; the learned blocks are
%%|   the same kind of object in all three.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph B["GeoTransolver / Transolver"]
        direction TB
        B1["per point: centered coordinates, unit normal<br/>global: the far-field vector (a unit direction under the protocol)"]:::data
        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>global-context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: pressure, wall shear"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction TB
        I1["per point: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["invariant seed; length unit = RMS pairwise distance"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["linear head on invariants → equivariant basis"]:::fixed
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
    end
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface point
it receives the coordinates, centered on the case, and the unit normal as a
six-channel feature. The far-field vector is a three-channel global feature.
Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through a
dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention. The
ball-query local-feature path is off throughout this program, because it is
off in the recipe's shipped configuration. The GeoTransolver compared here
is therefore the one a user gets by running the recipe unmodified, not the
strongest configuration the class can express. It is not rotation- or
translation-equivariant. Rotate the car and it sees a different input
(@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal. The far-field vector is broadcast to every point.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and measure weight per point and
each global direction as a unit vector, consumed only through invariants
and equivariant anchors (@sec-isla). @tbl-architectures gives the three
configurations side by side. The parameter counts and training footprints
are in @tbl-isla-cost. On the interior tasks the baseline is
GeoTransolver-volume, the recipe's volume configuration of the same class,
described with those tasks in @sec-interior.

**The reference configurations.** Every standing in the book holds one
configuration per architecture, selected by one rule: the most accurate
configuration of that architecture that trains under 80 GiB of peak device
memory per GPU on the two selection datasets, the DrivAerML Surface task and
the 210-wing HiLiftAeroML rung, each candidate trained for 500 epochs on two
seeds and scored at 200,000 cells, ties within 3% of the best resolved
toward the cheaper candidate, and a disagreement between the two datasets
resolved by the smallest mean of error divided by the best error on each.
The configurations are: ISLA width 512, 12 layers, 512 slices, cosine
routing, the centered sample-conditioned prototypes, learning rate 3.75e-4,
trained at 200,000 cells; GeoTransolver width 256 (local width 32),
learning rate 1e-3, trained at 200,000 cells; Transolver width 512 with 16
layers at 100,000 cells, learning rate 1e-3. The selection itself is read in
@sec-scoreboard-200k and @sec-de-result. Lanes that hold other
configurations, the ladders and the capacity and scaling studies, name
theirs in every row and caption.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | the far-field vector through the global-context projector: a unit direction under the protocol | 12 | 256 | 256 |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | the far-field vector, broadcast per point: a unit direction under the protocol | 16 | 512 | 256 |
| ISLA | position, unit normal, measure weight, through invariants and anchors only | unit direction(s) and global scalars | 12 | 512 | 512 |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 200,000 sampled surface cells per
case under the reporting protocol. *Layers*: soft-slice attention blocks.
*Hidden*: width of the per-point feature. How to read this: the table
states what each model is handed, not how accurate it is or what it costs
(@sec-using-cost). Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

### Global directions enter as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars {#sec-unit-direction-rule}

**A problem's global conditions enter every architecture in one form:
directions as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars.** The rule is a property
of the problem, not of any dataset's units. A direction carries no scale.
Whatever scale the pipeline attaches to it (the units the solver ran in) is
an accident of the dataset, and a model would have to learn to ignore it. A
magnitude that matters physically, a far-field speed or a Reynolds number,
is a separate scalar with its own place in the input. ISLA enforces the
rule by construction: it normalizes its global vectors and takes magnitudes
only through rank-0 `global_schema` (@sec-isla-inputs). GeoTransolver and
Transolver consume whatever vector the pipeline hands them, so for them the
rule is a protocol requirement. Every dataset pipeline of the recipe
writes the far-field direction as a unit vector.

The motivating control is visible before training. GeoTransolver's
global-context projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the
vector directly, so its conditioning depends on the magnitude. At unit
magnitude a head of the untrained projector spreads over most of the 256
slices. At the magnitude of the HiLiftAeroML solver's velocity (in inches
per second) it routes almost all of its weight to one (@tbl-projector).
Transolver concatenates the raw vector into every point's features, with
the same hazard in a different place. Training can in principle rescale
either path, so these numbers are the initialization signature. The trained
measurement, in the collapsed note below, is what the rule rests on.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-projector
#| output: asis
cond = J("geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json")["results"]
out = "| magnitude of the global vector | occupied slices per head (entropy-equivalent, min to max over heads) | largest context entry |\n|---:|---|---:|\n"
labels = {1.0: "1 (unit direction)", 38.9: "38.9 (DrivAerML's velocity, m/s)", 2679.5054741899685: "2,679.5 (HiLiftAeroML's velocity, in/s)"}
for r in cond:
    lab = next(v for k, v in labels.items() if abs(k - r["drive_magnitude"]) < 1e-6)
    out += f"| {lab} | {r['effective_slices_min']:.1f} to {r['effective_slices_max']:.1f} of 256 | {r['context_abs_max']:.2f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Conditioning of GeoTransolver's global-context projector at initialization against the magnitude of the "
      "global vector it receives, at the recipe's projector dimensions with untrained weights. "
      "How to read this: a head that occupies one slice has lost its ability to condition on the direction; "
      "this is a property of the untrained network, and the trained consequence is in the note below. "
      "Data: results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-projector}")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The trained consequence, at the exploration budget"}
At 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same cases, seeds and budget in
both arms, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the unit direction are each more
accurate than their physical-velocity twin on every one of the 180
validation cases, by a median factor above three (@tbl-unit-vs-physical).
The table is a control on an input scale, measured at the exploration
budget of 10,000 cells. It makes no accuracy claim about any architecture
and appears nowhere else in the book.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unit-vs-physical
#| output: asis
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
ud = J("udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json")["paired"]
fp = lambda keys: [fp35[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver, physical velocity, lr 1e-3", fp([f"lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 1e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3 (its best at this rung)", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])),
    ("Transolver, physical velocity, lr 3e-3", fp([f"t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("Transolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
]
out = "| arm | surface pressure error, seed mean (seeds) |\n|---|---|\n"
for lab, v in arms:
    out += f"| {lab} | {mean(v):.4f} ({' / '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in v)}) |\n"
print(out)
g, t = ud["gt_physical_35_vs_gt_unit_35"], ud["transolver_physical_35_vs_transolver_unit_35"]
print(f": The input-scale control at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure "
      f"on the 180 shared validation cases, float32, final-epoch checkpoints, 10,000 cells (the exploration budget), 500 epochs. Paired per case, "
      f"the unit-direction GeoTransolver is lower than its physical-velocity twin on {g['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of "
      f"{g['n_cases']} cases (median factor {g['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}) and the unit-direction Transolver on "
      f"{t['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of {t['n_cases']} (median factor {t['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}). "
      f"How to read this: the physical-velocity rows measure an input scale, not an architecture; the unit-direction rows are the protocol. Data: "
      f"results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json, results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (paired counts). {{#tbl-unit-vs-physical}}")
```
:::

Three consequences follow. First, every architecture receives each global
direction as a unit vector and each magnitude as a scalar, and a comparison
against a baseline fed a raw vector is reported only as a measurement of the
input scale. Second, the unit-direction baseline is the reference baseline
on every rung. Third, the input scale is fixed by rule rather than by
control, because learning-rate, training-length and seed controls vary the
optimizer and cannot detect an input-scale defect. On the DrivAerML Surface
task and the DrivAerML Volume task, whose solver velocity is of order tens
of meters per second, the trained difference between the two inputs is
inside seed spread. The rule applies on every
dataset regardless, because a rule that depends on the dataset's units is
not a rule.

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book is produced under the
following rules. A comparison that violates one is not reported.** The
datasets are in @sec-datasets and their splits in @sec-splits, the metric
in @sec-metrics and the training recipe in @sec-protocol.

1. **Matched cells per case: 200,000 sampled surface cells for every
   architecture, the reporting protocol.** Accuracy is flat in the cell
   count above 100,000 for every model and is not below it
   (@sec-equal-budget), so a cell mismatch would be a handicap
   disguised as an architecture difference. A number at any other count
   carries its label.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm.** Doubling GeoTransolver's budget at
   the small rungs does not lower its error (@sec-data-efficiency). At
   435 cars and 200,000 cells, 1,000 epochs move neither ISLA nor
   GeoTransolver outside seed spread (@sec-equal-budget). So 500
   under-trains neither.
3. **Each architecture at its own best learning rate, chosen by
   validation.** ISLA runs at 1e-3 at width 192 and at the width rule's
   rate above it (@sec-using-lr). GeoTransolver receives a two-rate control,
   1e-3 and 3e-3, on every rung and is reported at the better rate. The
   search favors the baseline. At the reporting protocol its better rate is
   3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives each global direction as a unit vector and
   each magnitude as a scalar** (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually**, so the reader can
   see whether a ratio exceeds the seed spread.
6. **Shared validation cases**, sampled with the same seed, for every
   architecture.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed**: the count of
   validation cases on which one architecture is more accurate, with median
   and worst-decile per-case ratios, alongside the ratio of means.
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once**, taken verbatim from the dataset
   manifest; sealed per checkpoint, not per program (@sec-splits).
9. **Preregistered bars**: each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.
10. **Boundary conditions enter ISLA as boundary meshes with per-cell
    fields**, never as one-hot scalar fields on the interior mesh; a
    dataset configuration is checked against this before its first lane.
    GeoTransolver, which has no boundary-token path, receives the same
    labels and values as nodal fields (@sec-data-conventions).
11. **The stored signed-distance field and its gradient, computed from the
    boundary alone, are given to both ISLA and GeoTransolver** on every
    interior task; neither architecture receives a volume-mesh quantity
    the other does not.
12. **No architecture's reference lane trains with augmentation.** The
    rotation-augmented baselines of the posed evaluation are a labeled
    control (@sec-pose-contract), never a standing.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

**Every number in a family of comparisons is read from one fixed
instrument, and a control that changes the instrument is reported as a
control.** The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and
evaluation configuration. On the DrivAerML Surface task, it is surface
pressure and wall shear on 48 held-out cars at 200,000 sampled cells,
scored in float32. On the DrivAerML Volume task, it is pressure, velocity
and turbulent viscosity at the interior queries of the same 48 cars. On
HiLiftAeroML, it is pressure, velocity and wall shear on 180 held-out cases
shared by every training split, at the same count and precision. On
AirfRANS, it is pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity at the interior
queries of its 200 test airfoils. An instrument is never widened after a
result is read from it. A control that changes it (another cell count, a
rotated pose, a biased sampling density) is reported as such and never
mixed into an in-family number. Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a
small validation set and two seeds a thin noise estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**Every cross-architecture comparison states, on both sides, the parameter
count, the cells per case and the training memory, or says in the same
sentence where they differ and whether the difference could buy accuracy.**
The reference configurations are matched on one thing only, the 80 GiB
memory budget they were selected under, and differ in parameters, cells per
case and step time; each dataset chapter states those beside its standing,
and the training footprints on the selection task are in @sec-using-cost.
Memory is therefore the one controlled variable of the selection and no
accuracy result depends on it otherwise. The
checkpoints in this book are trained by implementations of the same
function that differ only in footprint. Where the two architectures are
compared at unequal parameters or memory, the section that does so says
which side has more and whether it bought accuracy (@sec-equal-budget).

## Learning rate {#sec-lr-protocol}

**Each architecture trains at its own best learning rate, and the rate is
part of the protocol, not a tuning afterthought.** In the reference
configurations GeoTransolver and Transolver run at 1e-3 and ISLA at 3.75e-4,
the width rule's rate at width 512 (@sec-using-lr). On the ladders, which
hold the 256-wide baselines and ISLA at 384 or 192 wide, GeoTransolver runs
at the better of 1e-3 and 3e-3 per rung, found by the two-rate control of
rule 3, Transolver at 3e-3, and ISLA at 5e-4 (384 wide) or 1e-3 (192 wide). Why ISLA's rate does not follow the
baselines' is a property of the routing form, explained once in
@sec-isla-routing-forms.

## Datasets {#sec-datasets}

**Seven datasets carry the evidence, each with its own chapter in Part III,
and all of them supply the same input schema: boundary cells with
positions, outward normals and measures, plus the problem's global
conditions and, where the problem has them, per-cell boundary data.** One
model implementation therefore runs on all of them. The aerodynamic sets
are instances of external aerodynamics with $K = 1$ global direction, the
far-field flow direction, and $S \in \{0, 1\}$ global scalars; the solids
and the brackets exercise the global scalars, the per-cell boundary
scalars and, on the lug, $K = 0$. Each chapter of Part III draws its
dataset on sample cases, states its diversity, and says what is measured on
it and what the dataset does not say. This section holds only what is
common to all of them: the roster, the file conventions and the split rule.

| dataset | what it is | what varies | global inputs | task | chapter |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DrivAerML** (cars) | 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants; time-averaged surface pressure and wall shear, plus volume fields | geometry only; one far-field condition | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | the Surface task and the Volume task | @sec-drivaerml |
| **HiLiftAeroML** (wings) | 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing geometries, each at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°; surface pressure, velocity and wall shear | geometry and far-field direction | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | surface, on nested training rungs, geometry holdouts and a fixed angle | @sec-hilift |
| **AirfRANS** (airfoils) | 1,001 two-dimensional incompressible RANS solutions around NACA airfoils; pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity in the volume | geometry, inlet direction and inlet speed | $K = 1$, $S = 1$ | interior | @sec-airfrans |
| **Shift-SUV** | sport-utility bodies in two rear-end families, estate and fastback; surface pressure and wall shear at a lower speed than DrivAerML | geometry; a speed shift common to every architecture | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | surface; a held-out family | @sec-shift-suv |
| **PLAID Tensile2d** | two-dimensional elasto-viscoplastic tension of a notched specimen; stress components, plastic strain and displacement at the nodes | the applied pressure and five material parameters; the shape barely | $K = 1$ (the load direction), $S = 6$ | interior (every node a query) | @sec-tensile2d |
| **GINOT Bracket Lug** | three-dimensional elastoplastic lugs clamped at one end and pressed in the hole; von Mises stress at the nodes | hole radius, length, thickness and pressure | $K = 0$, $S = 4$ | interior (every node a query) | @sec-lug |
| **DeepJEB++** | generated jet-engine brackets under four static load cases; von Mises stress and displacement on the surface | the shape, the load direction and the load kind | $K = 1$ (the load direction), $S = 2$ | surface | @sec-deepjeb |

: The datasets of the book and the chapter that owns each. *Global inputs*: $K$ unit directions and $S$ scalars (@sec-isla-inputs). How to read this: a row names what varies within the set, which fixes what a model trained on it must learn (@sec-parametric); the per-cell boundary scalars of the solids and brackets are listed in their chapters. {#tbl-datasets}

### Datasets beyond external aerodynamics {#sec-datasets-beyond-aero}

**The architecture is written for any steady boundary-driven PDE, and
external aerodynamics is its benchmark instance, not its scope.** The
three sets outside it, Tensile2d, the lug and DeepJEB++, are steady
problems whose loads and boundary conditions vary per sample, so they
exercise the global vector and scalar inputs and the per-cell boundary
scalars that the aerodynamic datasets leave at $K = 1$ and $n_b = 0$.
Every dataset enters the book's evidence only with GeoTransolver trained
on it under the fair-comparison protocol and a per-dataset preregistration
before its first lane; the open axis they represent is stated in
@sec-limits-datasets.

### Conventions shared by every dataset {#sec-data-conventions}

**A converted case is one native `DomainMesh` file (`.pdmsh`): an
`interior` point cloud, one or more named `boundaries`, and a
`global_data` dictionary.** The datasets differ in which of these the
model reads and in what the boundary cells carry.

- **Two reader layouts.** The *surface* datasets (DrivAerML Surface task,
  HiLiftAeroML, SHIFT-SUV, DeepJEB++) read only the boundary mesh: the
  reader walks into the boundary tensordict
  (`<case>.pdmsh/_tensordict/boundaries/<name>`), merges the parent
  file's `global_data` onto it (`MeshReaderWithGlobalData`), and the
  terminal transform `MeshToDomainMesh` places the prediction points at
  the cell centroids. The *interior* datasets (DrivAerML Volume task,
  (`DomainMeshReader`): the interior points are the queries and the
  boundary is kept whole whenever the cell budget exceeds its size.
- **Signed distance is positive outside the solid.** Interior nodes of a
  solid carry `sdf` $\le 0$; fluid points outside a body carry `sdf` $> 0$.
  `sdf_normals` is the gradient of that field, so it is the outward normal
  at the boundary. Converters negate a source that stores the opposite
  sign.
- **Boundary conditions are per-cell scalars.** Each labeled region is a
  0/1 indicator on the boundary cells (`bc_fixed`, `bc_loaded`,
  `bc_dirichlet`, …) and each prescribed value is a scalar on the cells it
  applies to and zero elsewhere (`bc_pressure`, `bc_value_g`, `bc_disp_x`,
  …). Where a traction vector exists it is stored too (`traction`,
  `bc_load`), but ISLA has no per-cell vector input. The traction on a
  pressed face is $-p\,n$, recoverable from the pressure scalar and the
  cell normal the model already sees. GeoTransolver has no boundary-token
  path, so the same labels and values are also written as nodal fields on
  the interior points (`tag_*`, `bc_*_node`) and enter its local embedding
  there.
- **Global vectors are unit directions and must be data of the problem.**
  For external aerodynamics `ComputeFreestreamDirection` writes `U_inf_dir`
  from the solver's velocity; for a loaded solid the load direction is the
  global vector. Where the targets are components in a fixed frame (the
  stress is predicted as a symmetric tensor and the components are read
  off it (@sec-isla-heads). Feeding the dataset's axes $+x, +y$ as global
  vectors is rejected: they are not a datum of the PDE (@sec-pose-prior). A dataset with no global
  direction ($K = 0$) runs ISLA with the eager geometry kernel; the fused
  kernel is written for $K = 1$.
- **Normalization statistics come from the manifest.** Every converter
  writes `manifest.json` next to the files with the named split lists and
  a `_stats` block of per-field mean and standard deviation pooled over the
  training split; the dataset yaml copies those values into
  `NormalizeMeshFields` (targets, and standardized input fields) and
  `StandardizeDomainGlobalField` (global scalars). Vector targets use one
  isotropic standard deviation (the Frobenius value divided by
  $\sqrt{2}$ in two dimensions), so a component's scale is not rescaled
  per axis.
- **Splits are named lists in the manifest; nested rungs are prefixes of
  one permutation.** Where a dataset publishes splits they are used
  unchanged (HiLiftAeroML, AirfRANS, SHIFT-SUV, PLAID's official ladder,
  set has to be carved out (Tensile2d), the draw is a fixed-seed
  permutation recorded in the manifest, and every smaller rung is a prefix
  of the larger one, so a rung differs from the next only by the cases it
  lacks.

| dataset | converter | dataset yaml | ISLA yaml |
|---|---|---|---|
| DrivAerML (Surface, Volume) | native files from the dataset release | recipe `datasets/drivaer_ml_surface.yaml`, `drivaer_ml_volume.yaml` | recipe `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml`, `isla_volume.yaml` |
| HiLiftAeroML | native files | recipe `datasets/highlift_surface.yaml` | recipe `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml` |
| SHIFT-SUV | native files | recipe `datasets/shift_suv_surface.yaml`, `shift_suv_estate_surface.yaml`, `shift_suv_fastback_surface.yaml` | as DrivAerML |
| AirfRANS | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_convert.py` | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_volume.yaml` | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/isla_volume_airfrans.yaml` |
| PLAID Tensile2d | `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/plaid_tensile2d_convert.py` | `…/datasets/plaid_tensile2d.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_tensile2d.yaml` |
| GINOT Bracket Lug | `…/datasets/ginot_lug_convert.py` | `…/datasets/ginot_lug_volume.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_lug.yaml` |
| DeepJEB++ | `…/datasets/deepjebpp_convert.py` | `…/datasets/deepjebpp_surface.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_surface_deepjebpp.yaml` |

: Where each dataset's conversion and configuration live. "Recipe" is the unified external-aerodynamics recipe root (`examples/cfd/external_aerodynamics/unified_external_aero_recipe`); `…/datasets/` abbreviates `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/`. The GeoTransolver yamls sit beside the ISLA yamls with the prefix `geotransolver_`. {#tbl-data-files}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-data-samples
#| output: asis
rows = [
    ("DrivAerML", "drivaer", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", "volume points", "n_interior_points"),
    ("HiLiftAeroML", "hilift", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", None, None),
    ("SHIFT-SUV (fastback)", "shift_suv", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", None, None),
    ("AirfRANS", "airfrans", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "interior points", "n_interior_points"),
    ("PLAID Tensile2d", "tensile2d", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
    ("GINOT Bracket Lug", "lug", "boundary triangles", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
    ("AeroZoo", "aerozoo", "boundary triangles (four condition types)", "n_boundary_cells", "volume points", "n_interior_points"),
]
out = "| dataset | sample case (split) | boundary | interior |\n|---|---|---:|---:|\n"
for name, key, blab, bkey, ilab, ikey in rows:
    m = meta[key]
    split = m.get("split", m.get("family", ""))
    b = f"{m[bkey]:,} {blab}"
    i = f"{m[ikey]:,} {ilab}" if ikey else "—"
    out += f"| {name} | `{m['case']}` ({split}) | {b} | {i} |\n"
print(out)
```

### Splits {#sec-splits}

**Every split in the book is either the dataset's curated manifest used
unchanged or a fixed-seed permutation recorded in the manifest, and a
sealed test split is evaluated once.** DrivAerML has one validation set of
48 cars, shared by the Surface and Volume tasks and by every experiment,
with a training set of 435 cars or a nested rung of 27, 54, 109 or 218
(@sec-car-ladder). HiLiftAeroML's manifests hold out one question each and
overlap, so a test split there is sealed per checkpoint and not per program
(@sec-data-hilift-splits). AirfRANS ships its `full`, `reynolds` and
`aoa` manifests (@sec-data-airfrans), Shift-SUV its two families
(@sec-data-shift-suv), and the solids and brackets use fixed-seed
permutations whose smaller rungs are prefixes of the larger ones
(@sec-data-tensile2d, @sec-data-lug, @sec-data-deepjeb).

## Protocol {#sec-protocol}

**One frozen recipe produces every cross-architecture number in the book.
A comparison that departs from it says so in the same sentence.**

| item | setting |
|---|---|
| cells per case | 200,000 sampled surface cells per case per step, the recipe default and the reporting protocol, every architecture and every dataset; on the interior tasks, 200,000 interior queries per case on DrivAerML and 100,000 on AirfRANS |
| exploration budget | 10,000 cells per case: appears only as a labeled rung of a cell-count ladder or as the labeled setting of a mechanism control, never as an accuracy standing |
| epochs and schedule | 500 epochs, one case per step; the learning rate is divided by ten every 100 epochs, so the effective budget is about 300 epochs at a useful rate |
| arithmetic | bfloat16 autocast in training; float32 at evaluation (@sec-metrics) |
| augmentation | none, for every architecture's reference lane; the rotation-augmented baselines of the posed evaluation are a labeled control (@sec-pose-contract) |
| boundary conditions | boundary meshes with per-cell fields for ISLA, the same labels and values as nodal fields for GeoTransolver (@sec-data-conventions) |
| signed distance | on the interior tasks the stored signed-distance field and its gradient, computed from the boundary alone, go to both ISLA and GeoTransolver |
| learning rate | each architecture at its own best rate at the reporting protocol: ISLA $10^{-3}$ at width 192 and the width rule's rate above it (@sec-using-lr), GeoTransolver and Transolver $3 \times 10^{-3}$; every row names the rate it uses (@sec-lr-protocol) |
| global inputs | each global direction as a unit vector, each magnitude as a scalar, for every architecture (@sec-unit-direction-rule) |
| seeds | two or more (42 and 43 unless stated), reported individually beside the mean |
| checkpoint | the final epoch; no selection on validation error |
| datasets | a result counts when it is reproduced on two datasets; a single-dataset result is labeled as such |
| validation and test | all architectures at all rungs scored on the same validation cases; a sealed test split is evaluated exactly once with the checkpoint and configuration declared in writing beforehand |
| preregistration | every experiment states its prediction and its falsifier in readout units before it runs; the dated record is the notebook (@sec-notebook) |

Because the rungs of a ladder share one rate and one schedule, a difference
between rungs is a difference in data and nothing else. When a result
favors one architecture, the strongest controls for the other (a higher
learning rate, doubled epochs, a same-family architecture without the
geometry encoder) run under the same recipe before the result is stated.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="What the validation set is used for"}
The HiLiftAeroML and DrivAerML accuracy figures in this book are
validation-set figures with no checkpoint selection behind them, and with
this much adaptive reuse disclosed. The per-architecture learning rate is
chosen on the full split by validation. Transolver's rate is chosen per
small-data rung on it. The ablations that follow earlier readouts are
designed after reading it. The choice of which results to present is made
with it in view. The HiLiftAeroML test splits are spent only on the
regime-extrapolation evaluations and one diagnostic run alongside them (a
variant of ISLA given raw coordinates). Because those test sets cover every
geometry (@sec-splits), the remaining test manifests are held out per
checkpoint but are not program-level confirmations (@sec-limits-validation).
:::

Every figure and table caption ends with the artifact in `results/` from
which it is computed, and every figure is drawn from that artifact at render
time.
